Basal metabolic rate measurements in the Ash-grey mouse (Pseudomys albocinereus) provide key insights into the energetic strategies of this small, nocturnal murid rodent. Respirometry trials conducted under standard resting conditions at a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] have established a maximum oxygen consumption of 43.52 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 43.52 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This relatively modest metabolic rate aligns with expectations for a desert-adapted species that must conserve energy during periods of scarce resources. The value, derived from flow-through respirometry on individuals in post-absorptive state within their thermoneutral zone, offers a robust empirical baseline for understanding daily energetic expenditure.

Female Ash-grey mice typically attain a maximum adult body mass of 40 grams [Wwi = 40 grams], though considerable variation exists across populations, with some individuals reaching only around 15 grams in marginal habitats. This ultimate wet weight for females represents the upper limit of somatic growth under favorable resource conditions. In contrast, newborn pups emerge from the birth canal weighing a mere 4 grams [Wwb = 4 grams], a neonatal mass that reflects the altricial state of the newborns at parturition. Such a substantial disparity between birth weight and asymptotic adult mass underscores the rapid growth trajectory that must be sustained during the suckling period.

Reproductive output in the Ash-grey mouse is comparatively high for a small conilurine rodent, with females exhibiting a maximum litter size of 2 to 6 pups per litter [N_R_i = 2 to 6 pups per litter]. This litter size is achieved multiple times within a breeding season, as females can produce up to 3 litters per year [F_R_i = up to 3 litters per year] when conditions are favorable. The gestation period, measured under controlled thermal conditions at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], lasts approximately 37.5 days [tg = approximately 37.5 days], a value at the upper end of the typical range reported for congeners.

Developmental milestones in Pseudomys albocinereus follow a predictable schedule under favorable thermal conditions, with key transitions occurring at remarkably precise intervals when body temperature is maintained at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. Weaning, defined as the cessation of lactation and the onset of nutritional independence, occurs at 26 days since birth [tx = 26 days since birth] at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. Following this dietary transition, the juveniles enter a period of rapid somatic growth and behavioral maturation. Puberty, marking the onset of gonadal activity and the capacity for reproductive activation, is reached at 146 days since birth [tp = 146 days since birth], a relatively delayed schedule that reflects the extended investment in structural growth before the initiation of breeding activity at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C].

Longevity estimates for the Ash-grey mouse, extrapolated from life-table data for the closely related Pseudomys australis, suggest a maximum lifespan of approximately 7.9 years [am = approximately 7.9 years] under controlled captive conditions at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This represents a substantial lifespan for a rodent of this body size, exceeding the typical one-to-two-year expectancy of many small murids. Such longevity is ecologically significant, as it allows for repeated reproductive opportunities across multiple breeding seasons, thereby offsetting the species' moderately small litter sizes. The combination of a delayed reproductive maturation and a multi-year reproductive window suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes adult survival and iteroparity over a single, high-investment reproductive bout.
